results.identificationRemarks: > Gall formation by T. tambotis is confined to the sterns of S. africana, with one to several galls, which vary greatly in size, being formed per stem. Apart from T. tambotis, which is the most common and numerically dominant insect associated with these galls, three other species have occasionally been found. These in- dude two other chalcidoid species, Ormyrus sp. (Ormyridae) and Bruchophagus sp. (Eurytomidae), and an undetermined species of Sesiidae (Lepi- doptera). The biologies of these species have not been studied in detail, but initial observations indicate that Ormyrus sp. is parasitic on the larvae of T. tambotis. Tanaostigmodes tambotis is gregarious, with up to 60 pupae being recorded from a single gall. The larvae live separately in tunnels in the plant tissue and, on pupation, become encapsulated in closed chambers. Emergence takes place between October and January, with each adult escaping through its own emergence hole. Males are the first to appear and their numbers seem to peak during November, followed by a peak in female numbers about one month later.

results.occurrenceRemarks: Spiky, spherical galls growing on Catclaw Acacia shrub in a riparian desert canyon. Link to host plant Catclaw Acacia observation: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/255454174 Tanaostigmodes howardii is an insect in Chalcidoid Wasps (Chalcidoidea) superfamily. It lays egg(s) on Catclaw Acacia (Senegalia greggii) which induces the host plant to form the gall(s). The galls are "detachable, round, monothalamous and are often found in clusters along the stems of Catclaw Acacia. The surface of these galls is broken into plates, with a small thorn or bristle emanating from each plate. Galls measure 5mm across and are gray-green, similar to stem. Some have a bark-like texture." Plant Galls of the Western United States, Ronald Russo, pp. 45-46, plate 19, p.233, figure 67, and plates 391, 392. Gallformers: https://www.gallformers.org/gall/3235 BugGuide: https://bugguide.net/index.php?q=search&keys=Tanaostigmodes%20howardii My Chalcidoid Wasps (Chalcidoidea) superfamily observations: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?taxon_id=69750&user_id=aparrot1&verifiable=any xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx What is a GALL? Gallformers: https://www.gallformers.org/ "Plant galls are abnormal growths of plant tissues, similar to tumors or warts in animals, that have an external cause--such as an insect, mite, nematode, virus, fungus, bacterium, or even another plant species. Growths caused by genetic mutations are not galls. Nor are lerps and other constructions on a plant that do not contain plant tissue. Plant galls are often complex structures that allow the insect or mite that caused the gall to be identified even if that insect or mite is not visible." GALLS (Insect-induced) references: Plant Galls of the Western United States: a photographic guide to 536 species of plant galls found west of the Rockies, with 400+ color images and plates, Ronald A. Russo, April 2021. Gallformers: Identify Galls by name or by host plant https://www.gallformers.org/id Galls of California: an INaturalist Project, https://www.inaturalist.org/projects/galls-of-california BugGuide: Arthropods: Photos of Insects, Spiders & Their Kin (US & Canada), clickable categories or use search bar (scientific name): https://bugguide.net/node/view/3/bgpage

Hiking into the coastal strand habitat. I wanted to hike further into the interior but I was worried about not being able to charge my phone since it got wet the day before and didn't want to get turned around without a GPS. Seen on a three day solo camping trip to East Cape in Everglades National Park (Cape Sable). I was particularly excited to go shelling on the beach (did not collect any shells, as that is prohibited in ENP) and also try some blacklighting out there. All of my observations from this trip: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?d1=2022-11-21&d2=2022-11-23&order=asc&place_id=any&user_id=joemdo My mollusk observations from this trip: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?d1=2022-11-21&d2=2022-11-23&order=asc&place_id=any&taxon_id=47115&user_id=joemdo My blacklighting observations from this trip: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?d1=2022-11-21&d2=2022-11-23&order=asc&place_id=any&project_id=blacklighting-florida&user_id=joemdo Gonna be a while before I finish posting everything and before I finish writing up this journal post summing up the trip but eventually there will be more info here: https://www.inaturalist.org/journal/joemdo/72888-nov-21-nov-23-2022-east-cape-sable-camping I am also planning on posting some videos to youtube over the next week or so but I'm prioritizing adding my observations first! Here's a link to my channel in case you want to see subscribe to see some videos about this trip: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC1Exy70GX48bo6JCDqqRrtw
